title: The Diamond Sutra, second half
tomorrow: is choosing between two good things really a problem?

cards: An engagement ring gets a diamond for a reason: the hardest stone there is, the one meant to last.
And the Diamond Sutra, named for that hardness, finishes its second half with a list of the softest, shortest things anyone could name. Stars at dawn. A lamp.
A bubble. A dream. A flash of lightning.
A cloud. And dew. Why would a sutra named for a diamond end in dew?

teach.b: Read the second half straight through and the puzzle starts to solve itself. The cutting keeps going. Past mind can't be grasped, present mind can't be grasped, future mind can't be grasped.

The teaching is equal, the sutra says, with nothing high and nothing low in it. Whoever looks for the Buddha in a body or a voice, a verse warns, is on the wrong road. Then a turn that's easy to miss.
Don't think, the Buddha tells Subhuti, that those on this path teach that things are cut off into nothing. The blade doesn't leave a pile of nothing behind. That's the key.
The diamond is the cutting: the tool that slices through every grip on things as fixed, solid, mine, forever. Dew is what you see once the cutting's done.
A drop that's really there, really wet, really catching light, and gone by mid-morning.

The closing verse, in paraphrase, says to look on everything made like stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud. So the hardest thing and the softest thing aren't opposites here.
One is the knife, the other is the view.
A diamond that ends in dew is a sutra that finishes its own work: nothing to hold forever, and everything worth seeing while it shines.

how: The Diamond Sutra's closing verse of passing things is often recited on its own in Mahayana communities, and some recite it at funerals and memorials.

o: a sutra on how to find and polish precious stones
a Mahayana text that cuts every grip, ending on dew
a story of a king who gave away his crown jewels

games.q: the second half — tap the pairs.
p: the knife that cuts the grip

s: the Diamond Sutra teaches that everything is cut off into nothing
the Buddha tells Subhuti not to think so. the cutting doesn't end in nothing.
the closing verse compares all that is made to dew and a bubble
stars, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud.
the sutra says the Buddha is found by his body and voice
a verse warns that seeking the Buddha by form or sound is the wrong road.

games.q: a perfect evening with friends ends, and your friend says, 'what's the point if it's over already?' what does the closing verse suggest?
o: like dew: it was really there, and its passing doesn't erase it.
nothing: since it ended, it was never really real at all.
plan the next one fast so the good feeling never ends.
games.why: dew is real and passing at once. the verse asks for that double view, not for clinging and not for calling it fake.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and watch thoughts come and go the way you'd watch weather. Each one, a plan, a worry, a song stuck in your head, is really there, and passing.
Don't hold it, don't push it; let it shine and dry like dew, and wait for the next, until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Diamond Sutra, second half: the cutting goes on, and then a verse of passing things, stars, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dew or frost, one of the passing things in the Diamond Sutra's closing verse.

carryVoice: For the road: like dew, really here and already passing. The whole diamond, read through.

sources.ref: Vajracchedika (Diamond Sutra), sections 18, 23, 26, 27 (ungraspable mind; equal, no high or low; not by form or sound; not annihilation)
